newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA WEIGHS DUAL MINERAL RIGHTS TRADITION.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA WEIGHS DUAL MINERAL RIGHTS TRADITION.

text.p: Mineral and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna said on Wednesday that South Africa's system of parallel public and private ownership of mineral rights needed to be overhauled to unlock the country's wealth.

Answering questions during a mini-debate in parliament, he said he found it difficult to accept suggestions in a draft green paper recently presented to him that the present system of mineral rights should be retained.
He said this approach assumed that there were willing sellers as well as blacks with enough money to buy mineral rights, adding: "That is not the reality that is confronting us in this country."

"As a self-respecting citizen of South Africa, and as an African, I am not going to associate myself with any notion that this government must accept that this dual system of the distribution of mineral rights in this country is there to stay.

"We are the only country where this dual system is pursued.... This developed during the heyday of both colonialism and apartheid where blacks...were prevented by law and policy from wning mineral rights."
Maduna said there were practical and constitutional constraints to changing the situation.
"The practical considerations are that if we are to touch the current configuration, we would not as the fiscus, be able to pay in order to take those mineral rights," he said.
"The constitutional aspect is that, whether we like it or not, mineral rights are actually part and parcel of what is protected by the property clause.

"But I am not suggesting that we are incapable of addressing this problem. I am suggesting that indeed something ought to be done by all of us to wrench these mineral rights from this system so that they could be equitably distributed (and) so that we could also use them to attract and encourage foreign investors who are currently alienated from coming in.
"There is no big scale mining entity that has come in since 1994 because mineral rights are inacessible to them, inasmuch as no small scale miner of serious size had benefited as a result," he said.
Some mining houses had told him "that while they are sitting on this wealth, their plans are not to mine in the next 20 or 30 years."
This was unacceptable given South Africa's high levels of poverty and unemployment, he said.
